summary: Reports simulation studies of what happens to TCP performance when the initial window size is increased. It supports the proposal to allow a larger initial window. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Before changing a rule, scientists test it in a pretend world. This report is the result of those pretend tests for letting TCP start faster.

questions: what do simulations show about larger tcp initial windows
does a larger tcp initial window help web browsing
what did ns-2 simulations show about tcp initial window
subtitle: Simulations of what happens to web and file-transfer traffic when TCP starts with up to four segments instead of one.

tldr.problem: A proposal would raise TCP's initial window from one segment to three or four, but people worried about its usefulness and about its effect on other traffic.
tldr.mechanism: The authors simulated a bottleneck link shared by web and file-transfer clients in ns-2, varying the initial window from one to four segments.
tldr.outcome: Web page delays dropped, often by about 30 percent, and file transfers were essentially unaffected. The authors conclude that an initial window of 3 packets (4380 bytes) improves perceived performance.

today: RFC 2415 is an Informational report and the unit metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it. It is a simulation study and defines no protocol.

sections.title: Why Study a Larger Initial Window
sections.content:
The tcp-impl working group had been discussing an increase in the permissible initial window (IW) of a TCP connection from one segment to three or four. A proposal to raise IW to about 4K bytes (4380 bytes with 1460-byte segments) raised concerns about both its usefulness and its effect on other traffic.

Earlier studies had shown benefits for single connections but not with a wide variety of simultaneous traffic. The authors set out to find when a larger IW is a win and what effect it has on other flows that still use an IW of one segment.
sections.eli5: TCP normally starts by sending one packet and speeds up slowly. People wondered if starting with a few packets would be faster, and whether it would be unfair to others.

sections.title: The Simulation Setup
sections.content:
The simulations used the public ns-2 simulator. Four client nodes and four server nodes each connect over 10 Mbps links to two routers joined by a 1.5Mb, 50ms bottleneck link. Clients download files by FTP or browse the web.

Every FTP transfer was a 1-MB file, and every web page had exactly three embedded URLs. Web clients requested a new page after a random delay uniformly distributed between 1 and 5 seconds. The maximum TCP window was 11 packets, segments were 1460 bytes and buffers held 25 packets. A dropped packet restarts with a window of one segment, as in current practice.

Runs used 8, 16 or 32 web clients with 0 to 3 FTP clients, an IW from 1 to 4, and a simulated run time of 360 seconds. The measures were goodput, median page delay and median file transfer delay.
sections.eli5: The authors built a pretend internet with one narrow road in the middle. Some pretend people downloaded big files and others clicked through web pages, and the authors counted who got through fastest.

sections.title: What the Simulations Showed
sections.content:
A larger IW had no detectable effect on 1-MB file transfers, so the study focuses on web connections. Median web page delay improved clearly as IW grew, in many cases by around 30%. The big step from IW of 1 to IW of 2 comes mainly from file sizes: the median size of both primary and in-line URLs fits completely into two packets.

Packet drop rates rose with IW, but except in the single most pathological overload the rise was less than 1%. Because performance improved even as drops rose slightly, the authors say drop rate is not an indicator of user-level performance.

Using network power (goodput divided by median delay), going from IW 1 to IW 4 raised it by at least 15% even in a congested, bulk-transfer-dominated case, and by up to 60% where web traffic dominated. Concurrent file transfers essentially kept the same network power, though web transfers could gain slightly more bandwidth.
sections.eli5: Starting with a few packets made web pages load faster, often about a third faster. Big downloads going on at the same time hardly noticed.

sections.title: HTTP 1.1 and Mixed Window Sizes
sections.content:
A rough HTTP 1.1 model sent the primary URL and the three embedded URLs over one connection. The steep gain from IW 1 to 2 smoothed out. Occasionally going from IW 3 to 4 reduced network power, which suggests that raising IW above 4 may not always help in a very congested network.

In a half-and-half experiment, some web clients used IW 1 and others IW 3. With 8/8 and 16/16 splits, the mixture had no negative effect on the IW 1 conversations, and the IW 3 conversations kept their performance. In the extremely congested 32/32 split, the IW 3 connections were adversely affected, which the authors attribute to many connections opening at once and suffering multiple packet losses.
sections.eli5: When some kids start fast and others start slow, the slow kids were not hurt in normal crowds. In a really jammed hallway, the fast starters got bumped more.

sections.title: Conclusions and Caveats
sections.content:
The authors conclude that raising the initial window to 3 packets (or 4380 bytes) helps perceived performance. They released their models and scripts so others can run more variations.

They also tried RED queue management in ns-2 but did not report it as complete. Adding RED to the bottleneck gave performance gains similar to a larger IW, with an IW of 1. The simulations used a T1 link; the authors expect the results to scale to higher bandwidth, and leave that for readers to investigate.
sections.eli5: Their answer: starting with three packets seems like a good idea. They shared their tools so other people can double-check.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document reports a simulation study of a proposed change to TCP, so it has no security considerations of its own. The authors also know of no security considerations attached to the proposed change.
sections.eli5: This is only a report about tests, and nobody found a safety problem.
